Part 2 (modB) · Linear Algebra and Geometry · Channels A, B and C · Lesson L19

Scalar products I

So far you could add vectors and multiply them by a number. In this lesson you learn to "multiply" two vectors and get a number: the scalar product, from which lengths, angles and perpendicularity will come. You will see the Euclidean scalar product ⟨x,y⟩=x1y1+⋯+xnyn\langle x, y\rangle = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n⟨x,y⟩=x1​y1​+⋯+xn​yn​, the products that come from a symmetric matrix, gS(x,y)=tx S yg_S(x, y) = {}^tx\,S\,ygS​(x,y)=txSy, and how every scalar product becomes a matrix as soon as you fix a basis.

The lesson in 8 points

  • In the lessons on scalar products the field is always K=R\K = \RK=R: you need the order (knowing whether a number is positive) and the square roots of positive numbers.
  • A scalar product takes two vectors v,wv, wv,w and returns a real number ⟨v,w⟩\langle v, w\rangle⟨v,w⟩. It must be bilinear (linear in the first slot and in the second) and symmetric (⟨v,w⟩=⟨w,v⟩\langle v, w\rangle = \langle w, v\rangle⟨v,w⟩=⟨w,v⟩). As a consequence ⟨v,0⟩=0\langle v, 0\rangle = 0⟨v,0⟩=0 for every vvv.
  • A scalar product is positive definite if ⟨v,v⟩>0\langle v, v\rangle > 0⟨v,v⟩>0 for every v≠0v \neq 0v=0; it is degenerate if there is a v≠0v \neq 0v=0 with ⟨v,w⟩=0\langle v, w\rangle = 0⟨v,w⟩=0 for every www. Positive definite implies non-degenerate, but not the other way round.
  • The model for everything is the Euclidean scalar product of Rn\R^nRn: ⟨x,y⟩=tx y=x1y1+⋯+xnyn\langle x, y\rangle = {}^tx\,y = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n⟨x,y⟩=txy=x1​y1​+⋯+xn​yn​. For example ⟨(1,3),(−2,1)⟩=−2+3=1\langle (1, 3), (-2, 1)\rangle = -2 + 3 = 1⟨(1,3),(−2,1)⟩=−2+3=1. It is positive definite.
  • Every symmetric matrix SSS gives a scalar product on Rn\R^nRn: gS(x,y)=tx S y=∑i,jxiSijyjg_S(x, y) = {}^tx\,S\,y = \sum_{i,j} x_iS_{ij}y_jgS​(x,y)=txSy=∑i,j​xi​Sij​yj​. The entry SijS_{ij}Sij​ is the coefficient of xiyjx_iy_jxi​yj​, and gS(ei,ej)=Sijg_S(e_i, e_j) = S_{ij}gS​(ei​,ej​)=Sij​.
  • Once a basis B={v1,…,vn}\mathcal B = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}B={v1​,…,vn​} is fixed, every scalar product ggg has an associated matrix [g]B[g]_{\mathcal B}[g]B​, symmetric, with entries g(vi,vj)g(v_i, v_j)g(vi​,vj​).
  • With the associated matrix everything is computed in coordinates: g(v,w)=t[v]B [g]B [w]Bg(v, w) = {}^t[v]_{\mathcal B}\,[g]_{\mathcal B}\,[w]_{\mathcal B}g(v,w)=t[v]B​[g]B​[w]B​.
  • At the exam the typical question is: "given the scalar product ggg and the basis B\mathcal BB, what is [g]B[g]_{\mathcal B}[g]B​?", also on spaces of polynomials. It is solved entry by entry.

Channels A, B and C

The Linear Algebra and Geometry handouts are the same for channels A, B and C (Buzano teaches in channels A and B, Radeschi in channels B and C), so these notes hold for all three. Only the days of the lessons change: the announcements are on the course's Moodle page (MDAG2, id 3831). Exam and quiz are the same for everyone.

§1

Why a product between vectors is needed

p. 96

With what you know from lessons L05–L18 you can add vectors and multiply them by a number. But you cannot yet say how long a vector is, nor whether two vectors are perpendicular, nor what angle they form. These are the questions of geometry, and to answer them you need a new operation.

At school (or in physics) you may have seen the "scalar product" of two vectors of the plane: you multiply the corresponding coordinates and add the results. With u=(1,3)u = (1, 3)u=(1,3) and v=(−2,1)v = (-2, 1)v=(−2,1):

u⋅v=1⋅(−2)+3⋅1=−2+3=1.u \cdot v = 1 \cdot (-2) + 3 \cdot 1 = -2 + 3 = 1.u⋅v=1⋅(−2)+3⋅1=−2+3=1.

Two vectors go in, a number comes out. Now fix u=(2,1)u = (2, 1)u=(2,1) and look at what happens when you change the second vector:

vvv⟨u,v⟩\langle u, v\rangle⟨u,v⟩What you see in the drawing
a=(1,2)a = (1, 2)a=(1,2)2⋅1+1⋅2=42 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 2 = 42⋅1+1⋅2=4aaa forms an acute angle with uuu
b=(−1,2)b = (-1, 2)b=(−1,2)2⋅(−1)+1⋅2=02 \cdot (-1) + 1 \cdot 2 = 02⋅(−1)+1⋅2=0bbb is perpendicular to uuu
c=(−2,1)c = (-2, 1)c=(−2,1)2⋅(−2)+1⋅1=−32 \cdot (-2) + 1 \cdot 1 = -32⋅(−2)+1⋅1=−3ccc forms an obtuse angle with uuu

The sign of this number already "knows" something about the angle between the two vectors: positive, zero, negative for acute, right, obtuse. In lesson L20 you will make it precise with the formula for the angle; here you build the foundation: what an operation must satisfy to deserve the name of scalar product.

Note · Why the field is R\RR for scalar products

The handouts warn that in this chapter, unlike the previous ones, the field is always K=R\K = \RK=R, for two reasons:

  • you need the order: saying that a number is positive (⟨v,v⟩>0\langle v, v\rangle > 0⟨v,v⟩>0). In C\CC there is no order (lesson L02);
  • you need the square root of a positive number, to define the length ⟨v,v⟩\sqrt{\langle v, v\rangle}⟨v,v⟩​ in lesson L20. In Q\QQ, for example, 2\sqrt 22​ is missing (lesson L01).

So all the vector spaces of these lessons are real. (In lesson L25 you will see the complex version, the Hermitian product.)

§2

The definition of scalar product

p. 96

Definition 19.1 · Scalar product

Let VVV be a real vector space. A scalar product on VVV is a map

V×V⟶R,(v,w)⟼⟨v,w⟩V \times V \longrightarrow \R, \qquad (v, w) \longmapsto \langle v, w\rangleV×V⟶R,(v,w)⟼⟨v,w⟩

that satisfies the following axioms:

  1. ⟨v+v′,w⟩=⟨v,w⟩+⟨v′,w⟩\langle v + v', w\rangle = \langle v, w\rangle + \langle v', w\rangle⟨v+v′,w⟩=⟨v,w⟩+⟨v′,w⟩,
  2. ⟨λv,w⟩=λ⟨v,w⟩\langle \lambda v, w\rangle = \lambda\langle v, w\rangle⟨λv,w⟩=λ⟨v,w⟩,
  3. ⟨v,w⟩=⟨w,v⟩\langle v, w\rangle = \langle w, v\rangle⟨v,w⟩=⟨w,v⟩,

for every v,v′,w,w′∈Vv, v', w, w' \in Vv,v′,w,w′∈V and every λ∈R\lambda \in \Rλ∈R.

Piece by piece:

  • V×VV \times VV×V is the set of ordered pairs (v,w)(v, w)(v,w) of vectors of VVV: the scalar product receives two vectors.
  • The arrow towards R\RR says that the result is a real number, not a vector. The symbol ⟨v,w⟩\langle v, w\rangle⟨v,w⟩ (angle brackets) is read "scalar product of vvv and www".
  • Axiom (1) says that you can split a sum in the first slot: adding and then multiplying gives the same result as multiplying and then adding.
  • Axiom (2) says that a number in the first slot comes out: ⟨3v,w⟩=3⟨v,w⟩\langle 3v, w\rangle = 3\langle v, w\rangle⟨3v,w⟩=3⟨v,w⟩.
  • Axiom (3), symmetry, says that the order of the two vectors does not matter.
  • "For every v,v′,w,w′v, v', w, w'v,v′,w,w′ and every λ\lambdaλ": the rules must hold always, for all vectors and all real numbers, not only in some lucky case.

Pitfall · Scalar product and multiplication by a scalar

They are two different things. Multiplication by a scalar (lesson L05) takes a number and a vector and returns a vector: 3⋅(1,2)=(3,6)3 \cdot (1, 2) = (3, 6)3⋅(1,2)=(3,6). The scalar product takes two vectors and returns a number: ⟨(1,2),(3,6)⟩=3+12=15\langle (1, 2), (3, 6)\rangle = 3 + 12 = 15⟨(1,2),(3,6)⟩=3+12=15.

The consequences of the axioms

The handouts observe that the rules "on the right" also follow from the three axioms:

  1. ⟨v,w+w′⟩=⟨v,w⟩+⟨v,w′⟩\langle v, w + w'\rangle = \langle v, w\rangle + \langle v, w'\rangle⟨v,w+w′⟩=⟨v,w⟩+⟨v,w′⟩,
  2. ⟨v,λw⟩=λ⟨v,w⟩\langle v, \lambda w\rangle = \lambda\langle v, w\rangle⟨v,λw⟩=λ⟨v,w⟩.

Here is why, one step at a time (above the equals sign there is the axiom used):

⟨v,w+w′⟩=(3)⟨w+w′,v⟩=(1)⟨w,v⟩+⟨w′,v⟩=(3)⟨v,w⟩+⟨v,w′⟩,\begin{aligned} \langle v, w + w'\rangle &\overset{(3)}{=} \langle w + w', v\rangle \overset{(1)}{=} \langle w, v\rangle + \langle w', v\rangle \\ &\overset{(3)}{=} \langle v, w\rangle + \langle v, w'\rangle, \end{aligned}⟨v,w+w′⟩​=(3)⟨w+w′,v⟩=(1)⟨w,v⟩+⟨w′,v⟩=(3)⟨v,w⟩+⟨v,w′⟩,​
⟨v,λw⟩=(3)⟨λw,v⟩=(2)λ⟨w,v⟩=(3)λ⟨v,w⟩.\langle v, \lambda w\rangle \overset{(3)}{=} \langle \lambda w, v\rangle \overset{(2)}{=} \lambda\langle w, v\rangle \overset{(3)}{=} \lambda\langle v, w\rangle.⟨v,λw⟩=(3)⟨λw,v⟩=(2)λ⟨w,v⟩=(3)λ⟨v,w⟩.

Symmetry lets you "turn round" the vectors, use the rule on the first slot and then turn them round again.

Two words to remember:

  • axioms (1), (2), (4), (5) say that the product is bilinear: with the second vector fixed, it is linear in the first; with the first fixed, it is linear in the second;
  • axiom (3) says that it is symmetric.

The product with the zero vector is zero. For every v∈Vv \in Vv∈V we have ⟨v,0⟩=0\langle v, 0\rangle = 0⟨v,0⟩=0. Indeed, since 0=0+00 = 0 + 00=0+0, by axiom (4)

⟨v,0⟩=⟨v,0+0⟩=⟨v,0⟩+⟨v,0⟩.\langle v, 0\rangle = \langle v, 0 + 0\rangle = \langle v, 0\rangle + \langle v, 0\rangle.⟨v,0⟩=⟨v,0+0⟩=⟨v,0⟩+⟨v,0⟩.

Call a=⟨v,0⟩a = \langle v, 0\ranglea=⟨v,0⟩: you have found that a=a+aa = a + aa=a+a. Taking aaa away from both sides, what is left is 0=a0 = a0=a. By symmetry ⟨0,v⟩=0\langle 0, v\rangle = 0⟨0,v⟩=0 holds too.

A name for the product. When you want to give the scalar product a name, you denote it with a letter, g:V×V→Rg : V \times V \to \Rg:V×V→R, and write g(v,w)g(v, w)g(v,w) instead of ⟨v,w⟩\langle v, w\rangle⟨v,w⟩. It is useful when several different scalar products appear in the same discussion.

Beyond the handouts · A computation you will use often

With bilinearity and symmetry you expand the "square of a sum" as with numbers:

⟨v+w,v+w⟩=⟨v,v+w⟩+⟨w,v+w⟩=⟨v,v⟩+⟨v,w⟩+⟨w,v⟩+⟨w,w⟩=⟨v,v⟩+2⟨v,w⟩+⟨w,w⟩.\begin{aligned} \langle v + w, v + w\rangle &= \langle v, v + w\rangle + \langle w, v + w\rangle \\ &= \langle v, v\rangle + \langle v, w\rangle + \langle w, v\rangle + \langle w, w\rangle \\ &= \langle v, v\rangle + 2\langle v, w\rangle + \langle w, w\rangle. \end{aligned}⟨v+w,v+w⟩​=⟨v,v+w⟩+⟨w,v+w⟩=⟨v,v⟩+⟨v,w⟩+⟨w,v⟩+⟨w,w⟩=⟨v,v⟩+2⟨v,w⟩+⟨w,w⟩.​

The first step uses axiom (1), the second axiom (4) twice, the last one symmetry. It is the vector version of (a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2(a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2, and in lesson L20 it is needed to prove the triangle inequality.

Formulas that are (and are not) scalar products

To decide whether a formula is a scalar product you check bilinearity and symmetry. To say no, a single numerical example in which a rule fails is enough.

Example · A formula that works: g(x,y)=2x1y1+3x2y2g(x, y) = 2x_1y_1 + 3x_2y_2g(x,y)=2x1​y1​+3x2​y2​ on R2\R^2R2

Here x=(x1,x2)x = (x_1, x_2)x=(x1​,x2​) and y=(y1,y2)y = (y_1, y_2)y=(y1​,y2​).

  • Axiom (1). With x′=(x1′,x2′)x' = (x_1', x_2')x′=(x1′​,x2′​): g(x+x′,y)=2(x1+x1′)y1+3(x2+x2′)y2=(2x1y1+3x2y2)+(2x1′y1+3x2′y2)=g(x,y)+g(x′,y)g(x + x', y) = 2(x_1 + x_1')y_1 + 3(x_2 + x_2')y_2 = (2x_1y_1 + 3x_2y_2) + (2x_1'y_1 + 3x_2'y_2) = g(x, y) + g(x', y)g(x+x′,y)=2(x1​+x1′​)y1​+3(x2​+x2′​)y2​=(2x1​y1​+3x2​y2​)+(2x1′​y1​+3x2′​y2​)=g(x,y)+g(x′,y).
  • Axiom (2). g(λx,y)=2λx1y1+3λx2y2=λ(2x1y1+3x2y2)=λg(x,y)g(\lambda x, y) = 2\lambda x_1y_1 + 3\lambda x_2y_2 = \lambda(2x_1y_1 + 3x_2y_2) = \lambda g(x, y)g(λx,y)=2λx1​y1​+3λx2​y2​=λ(2x1​y1​+3x2​y2​)=λg(x,y).
  • Axiom (3). g(y,x)=2y1x1+3y2x2=g(x,y)g(y, x) = 2y_1x_1 + 3y_2x_2 = g(x, y)g(y,x)=2y1​x1​+3y2​x2​=g(x,y), because the product of numbers is commutative.

So ggg is a scalar product. For example g((1,1),(1,−1))=2⋅1⋅1+3⋅1⋅(−1)=−1g((1, 1), (1, -1)) = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot 1 \cdot (-1) = -1g((1,1),(1,−1))=2⋅1⋅1+3⋅1⋅(−1)=−1.

Example · Three formulas that do not work

  • g(x,y)=x1y2g(x, y) = x_1y_2g(x,y)=x1​y2​ is not symmetric: g(e1,e2)=1⋅1=1g(e_1, e_2) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1g(e1​,e2​)=1⋅1=1, but g(e2,e1)=0⋅0=0g(e_2, e_1) = 0 \cdot 0 = 0g(e2​,e1​)=0⋅0=0. (Here e1=(1,0)e_1 = (1, 0)e1​=(1,0) and e2=(0,1)e_2 = (0, 1)e2​=(0,1) are the vectors of the canonical basis.)
  • g(x,y)=x1y1+x2y2+1g(x, y) = x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 + 1g(x,y)=x1​y1​+x2​y2​+1 is not bilinear: g(0,0)=1g(0, 0) = 1g(0,0)=1, while a scalar product always gives ⟨v,0⟩=0\langle v, 0\rangle = 0⟨v,0⟩=0.
  • g(x,y)=x12y12g(x, y) = x_1^2y_1^2g(x,y)=x12​y12​ is not linear in the first slot: g(2e1,e1)=4g(2e_1, e_1) = 4g(2e1​,e1​)=4, while 2 g(e1,e1)=22\,g(e_1, e_1) = 22g(e1​,e1​)=2.
§3

Degenerate and positive definite products

p. 96

Not all scalar products behave well. Take on R2\R^2R2 the formula g(x,y)=x1y1g(x, y) = x_1y_1g(x,y)=x1​y1​: it is bilinear and symmetric, so it is a scalar product. But it ignores the second coordinate: the vector e2=(0,1)e_2 = (0, 1)e2​=(0,1) gives

g(e2,w)=0⋅w1=0for every w∈R2.g(e_2, w) = 0 \cdot w_1 = 0 \quad \text{for every } w \in \R^2.g(e2​,w)=0⋅w1​=0for every w∈R2.

A non-zero vector that gives zero with everything: it is a serious defect, because this product "does not see" e2e_2e2​. The handouts give a name to this defect and to the opposite property.

Definition 19.2 · Degenerate, positive definite

A scalar product on VVV is:

  • degenerate if there exists v≠0v \neq 0v=0 such that ⟨v,w⟩=0\langle v, w\rangle = 0⟨v,w⟩=0 for every w∈Vw \in Vw∈V;
  • positive definite if ⟨v,v⟩>0\langle v, v\rangle > 0⟨v,v⟩>0 for every non-zero v∈Vv \in Vv∈V.

Piece by piece:

  • Degenerate is about ⟨v,w⟩\langle v, w\rangle⟨v,w⟩ with any www: there is a non-zero vector that gives zero with all the vectors of the space, itself included. A product that is not degenerate is called non-degenerate: for every v≠0v \neq 0v=0 there is at least one www with ⟨v,w⟩≠0\langle v, w\rangle \neq 0⟨v,w⟩=0.
  • Positive definite is only about ⟨v,v⟩\langle v, v\rangle⟨v,v⟩, the product of a vector with itself: it must be strictly positive for every non-zero vector. (For v=0v = 0v=0 we always have ⟨0,0⟩=0\langle 0, 0\rangle = 0⟨0,0⟩=0.)

Proposition 19.3

A positive definite scalar product is not degenerate.

The handouts' explanation, step by step:

  1. Suppose by contradiction that the product is positive definite and degenerate.
  2. Since it is degenerate, there exists v≠0v \neq 0v=0 with ⟨v,w⟩=0\langle v, w\rangle = 0⟨v,w⟩=0 for every www.
  3. In particular you can choose w=vw = vw=v: you get ⟨v,v⟩=0\langle v, v\rangle = 0⟨v,v⟩=0.
  4. But v≠0v \neq 0v=0 and the product is positive definite, so ⟨v,v⟩>0\langle v, v\rangle > 0⟨v,v⟩>0. Contradiction: the product cannot be degenerate. □\square□

Example · Three scalar products on R2\R^2R2 compared

  • g(x,y)=x1y1+x2y2g(x, y) = x_1y_1 + x_2y_2g(x,y)=x1​y1​+x2​y2​ is positive definite: g(x,x)=x12+x22>0g(x, x) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 > 0g(x,x)=x12​+x22​>0 as soon as one coordinate is not zero.
  • g(x,y)=x1y1g(x, y) = x_1y_1g(x,y)=x1​y1​ is degenerate: e2≠0e_2 \neq 0e2​=0 and g(e2,w)=0g(e_2, w) = 0g(e2​,w)=0 for every www.
  • g(x,y)=x1y1−x2y2g(x, y) = x_1y_1 - x_2y_2g(x,y)=x1​y1​−x2​y2​ is not degenerate, but it is not positive definite. It is not positive definite because g(e2,e2)=0−1=−1<0g(e_2, e_2) = 0 - 1 = -1 < 0g(e2​,e2​)=0−1=−1<0. It is not degenerate because, given v=(a,b)≠0v = (a, b) \neq 0v=(a,b)=0, the vector w=(a,−b)w = (a, -b)w=(a,−b) gives
    g(v,w)=a⋅a−b⋅(−b)=a2+b2>0.g(v, w) = a \cdot a - b \cdot (-b) = a^2 + b^2 > 0.g(v,w)=a⋅a−b⋅(−b)=a2+b2>0.

Pitfall · The converse of Proposition 19.3 is false

"Non-degenerate" does not imply "positive definite": the last example, x1y1−x2y2x_1y_1 - x_2y_2x1​y1​−x2​y2​, shows it. Watch out for a second mistake too: in that product the vector v=(1,1)v = (1, 1)v=(1,1) has g(v,v)=1−1=0g(v, v) = 1 - 1 = 0g(v,v)=1−1=0 even though it is non-zero, and yet the product is not degenerate. To be degenerate you need a vector that gives zero with all vectors, not only with itself (g((1,1),(1,0))=1≠0g((1, 1), (1, 0)) = 1 \neq 0g((1,1),(1,0))=1=0). Martelli's book calls a vector with ⟨v,v⟩=0\langle v, v\rangle = 0⟨v,v⟩=0 isotropic.

x1y1+x2y2x_1y_1 + x_2y_2x1​y1​+x2​y2​noyesg(x,x)=x12+x22g(x, x) = x_1^2 + x_2^2g(x,x)=x12​+x22​
2x1y1+3x2y22x_1y_1 + 3x_2y_22x1​y1​+3x2​y2​noyesg(x,x)=2x12+3x22g(x, x) = 2x_1^2 + 3x_2^2g(x,x)=2x12​+3x22​

§4

Three scalar products on polynomials

p. 97

A scalar product does not live only on Rn\R^nRn. The handouts show an example on the space R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x] of polynomials with real coefficients of degree ≤2\le 2≤2, that is the polynomials a+bx+cx2a + bx + cx^2a+bx+cx2 (lessons L05–L07: it has dimension 3 and canonical basis {1,x,x2}\{1, x, x^2\}{1,x,x2}). The idea is to evaluate the polynomials at some points and multiply the values.

Example 19.4 · Three scalar products on R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x]

On the space R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x] of polynomials with real coefficients of degree ≤2\le 2≤2 consider the scalar product

⟨p,q⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)+p(2)q(2).\langle p, q\rangle = p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1) + p(2)q(2).⟨p,q⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)+p(2)q(2).

This scalar product is positive definite: ⟨p,p⟩=p(0)2+p(1)2+p(2)2>0\langle p, p\rangle = p(0)^2 + p(1)^2 + p(2)^2 > 0⟨p,p⟩=p(0)2+p(1)2+p(2)2>0 for every non-zero polynomial ppp of degree ≤2\le 2≤2, because such a polynomial cannot vanish at the three distinct values 0,1,20, 1, 20,1,2.

The scalar product ⟨p,q⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)\langle p, q\rangle = p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1)⟨p,q⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1) is instead degenerate: for p(x)=x(1−x)p(x) = x(1 - x)p(x)=x(1−x) we have ⟨p,q⟩=0\langle p, q\rangle = 0⟨p,q⟩=0 for every q∈R2[x]q \in \R_2[x]q∈R2​[x].

Finally ⟨p,q⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)−p(2)q(2)\langle p, q\rangle = p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1) - p(2)q(2)⟨p,q⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)−p(2)q(2) is not degenerate, but it is not positive definite: for p(x)=x−1p(x) = x - 1p(x)=x−1 we have ⟨p,p⟩=(−1)2−12=0\langle p, p\rangle = (-1)^2 - 1^2 = 0⟨p,p⟩=(−1)2−12=0.

Let us look at the three products one by one.

The first product: how it is computed. With p=xp = xp=x and q=x2q = x^2q=x2: the values of ppp at 0,1,20, 1, 20,1,2 are 0,1,20, 1, 20,1,2; those of qqq are 0,1,40, 1, 40,1,4. So

⟨x,x2⟩=0⋅0+1⋅1+2⋅4=9.\langle x, x^2\rangle = 0 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 4 = 9.⟨x,x2⟩=0⋅0+1⋅1+2⋅4=9.

With p=q=1+xp = q = 1 + xp=q=1+x (values 1,2,31, 2, 31,2,3): ⟨1+x,1+x⟩=1+4+9=14\langle 1 + x, 1 + x\rangle = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14⟨1+x,1+x⟩=1+4+9=14.

Why it is a scalar product. It is symmetric, because p(t)q(t)=q(t)p(t)p(t)q(t) = q(t)p(t)p(t)q(t)=q(t)p(t). It is bilinear because evaluating is linear: (p+p′)(t)=p(t)+p′(t)(p + p')(t) = p(t) + p'(t)(p+p′)(t)=p(t)+p′(t) and (λp)(t)=λp(t)(\lambda p)(t) = \lambda p(t)(λp)(t)=λp(t). For example, for axiom (1):

⟨p+p′,q⟩=∑t=0,1,2(p(t)+p′(t))q(t)=∑t=0,1,2p(t)q(t)+∑t=0,1,2p′(t)q(t)=⟨p,q⟩+⟨p′,q⟩.\begin{aligned} \langle p + p', q\rangle &= \sum_{t = 0, 1, 2} \big(p(t) + p'(t)\big)q(t) \\ &= \sum_{t = 0, 1, 2} p(t)q(t) + \sum_{t = 0, 1, 2} p'(t)q(t) \\ &= \langle p, q\rangle + \langle p', q\rangle. \end{aligned}⟨p+p′,q⟩​=t=0,1,2∑​(p(t)+p′(t))q(t)=t=0,1,2∑​p(t)q(t)+t=0,1,2∑​p′(t)q(t)=⟨p,q⟩+⟨p′,q⟩.​

Why it is positive definite. ⟨p,p⟩\langle p, p\rangle⟨p,p⟩ is a sum of three squares, so it is ≥0\ge 0≥0. It is 000 only if p(0)=p(1)=p(2)=0p(0) = p(1) = p(2) = 0p(0)=p(1)=p(2)=0, that is if ppp has three distinct roots. But by Theorem 4.6 (lesson L04) a non-zero polynomial of degree n≥1n \ge 1n≥1 has at most nnn roots, and a non-zero constant polynomial has none: a non-zero polynomial of degree ≤2\le 2≤2 has at most two roots. So ⟨p,p⟩=0\langle p, p\rangle = 0⟨p,p⟩=0 only for p=0p = 0p=0.

The second product is degenerate. With only two points the reasoning breaks down: p(x)=x(1−x)=x−x2p(x) = x(1 - x) = x - x^2p(x)=x(1−x)=x−x2 is a non-zero polynomial of degree 2 that vanishes both at 0 and at 1. Then for every qqq:

⟨p,q⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)=0⋅q(0)+0⋅q(1)=0.\langle p, q\rangle = p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1) = 0 \cdot q(0) + 0 \cdot q(1) = 0.⟨p,q⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)=0⋅q(0)+0⋅q(1)=0.

The third product is not positive definite. p(x)=x−1p(x) = x - 1p(x)=x−1 equals −1-1−1 at 0, 000 at 1 and 111 at 2, so

⟨p,p⟩=(−1)2+02−12=0\langle p, p\rangle = (-1)^2 + 0^2 - 1^2 = 0⟨p,p⟩=(−1)2+02−12=0

with p≠0p \neq 0p=0. (The handouts write (−1)2−12(-1)^2 - 1^2(−1)2−12 because the term p(1)2=0p(1)^2 = 0p(1)2=0 disappears.) Moreover: ⟨1,1⟩=1+1−1=1>0\langle 1, 1\rangle = 1 + 1 - 1 = 1 > 0⟨1,1⟩=1+1−1=1>0 and ⟨x,x⟩=0+1−4=−3<0\langle x, x\rangle = 0 + 1 - 4 = -3 < 0⟨x,x⟩=0+1−4=−3<0, so the values of ⟨p,p⟩\langle p, p\rangle⟨p,p⟩ can have both signs.

Beyond the handouts · Why the third product is not degenerate

The handouts state it without proof. Here is one way. Consider the three polynomials

q0=(x−1)(x−2)2,q1=2x−x2,q2=x(x−1)2.q_0 = \frac{(x - 1)(x - 2)}{2}, \quad q_1 = 2x - x^2, \quad q_2 = \frac{x(x - 1)}{2}.q0​=2(x−1)(x−2)​,q1​=2x−x2,q2​=2x(x−1)​.

Check the values: q0q_0q0​ equals 1,0,01, 0, 01,0,0 at 0,1,20, 1, 20,1,2; q1q_1q1​ equals 0,1,00, 1, 00,1,0; q2q_2q2​ equals 0,0,10, 0, 10,0,1. Then, for every ppp:

⟨p,q0⟩=p(0),⟨p,q1⟩=p(1),⟨p,q2⟩=−p(2).\langle p, q_0\rangle = p(0), \quad \langle p, q_1\rangle = p(1), \quad \langle p, q_2\rangle = -p(2).⟨p,q0​⟩=p(0),⟨p,q1​⟩=p(1),⟨p,q2​⟩=−p(2).

If ⟨p,q⟩=0\langle p, q\rangle = 0⟨p,q⟩=0 for every qqq, in particular for q0,q1,q2q_0, q_1, q_2q0​,q1​,q2​, then p(0)=p(1)=p(2)=0p(0) = p(1) = p(2) = 0p(0)=p(1)=p(2)=0 and, as above, p=0p = 0p=0. So no non-zero polynomial gives zero with everything: the product is not degenerate.

§5

The Euclidean scalar product

p. 97

The "school" product of the first section has a precise name.

Definition 19.5 · Euclidean scalar product

The Euclidean scalar product on Rn\R^nRn is defined as

⟨x,y⟩=tx y=∑i=1nxiyi.\langle x, y\rangle = {}^tx\,y = \sum_{i=1}^n x_iy_i.⟨x,y⟩=txy=i=1∑n​xi​yi​.

Piece by piece:

  • xxx and yyy are column vectors of Rn\R^nRn, that is n×1n \times 1n×1 matrices.
  • tx{}^txtx is the transpose of xxx (lesson L08): the same vector written as a row, a 1×n1 \times n1×n matrix.
  • tx y{}^tx\,ytxy is a row-by-column product between a 1×n1 \times n1×n matrix and an n×1n \times 1n×1 one: the result is a 1×11 \times 11×1 matrix, that is a number:
    tx y=(x1,…,xn)(y1⋮yn)=x1y1+x2y2+⋯+xnyn.{}^tx\,y = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{pmatrix} = x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 + \dots + x_ny_n.txy=(x1​,…,xn​)​y1​⋮yn​​​=x1​y1​+x2​y2​+⋯+xn​yn​.
  • The symbol ∑i=1nxiyi\sum_{i=1}^n x_iy_i∑i=1n​xi​yi​ means "sum of the products xiyix_iy_ixi​yi​ for iii going from 1 to nnn".

Examples:

  • in R2\R^2R2, as in the handouts: ⟨(13),(−21)⟩=1⋅(−2)+3⋅1=1\left\langle \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\right\rangle = 1 \cdot (-2) + 3 \cdot 1 = 1⟨(13​),(−21​)⟩=1⋅(−2)+3⋅1=1;
  • in R3\R^3R3: ⟨(1,2,3),(4,−5,6)⟩=4−10+18=12\langle (1, 2, 3), (4, -5, 6)\rangle = 4 - 10 + 18 = 12⟨(1,2,3),(4,−5,6)⟩=4−10+18=12;
  • in R4\R^4R4: ⟨(1,0,−1,2),(3,5,1,1)⟩=3+0−1+2=4\langle (1, 0, -1, 2), (3, 5, 1, 1)\rangle = 3 + 0 - 1 + 2 = 4⟨(1,0,−1,2),(3,5,1,1)⟩=3+0−1+2=4.

Proposition 19.6

The Euclidean scalar product is a positive definite scalar product on Rn\R^nRn.

The handouts do not give the proof; here it is, from Martelli's book (Proposition 7.1.5).

  1. Bilinearity. It comes from the properties of the matrix product. For axiom (1): t(x+x′) y=(tx+tx′) y=tx y+tx′ y{}^t(x + x')\,y = ({}^tx + {}^tx')\,y = {}^tx\,y + {}^tx'\,yt(x+x′)y=(tx+tx′)y=txy+tx′y. The other linearity axioms are checked in the same way.
  2. Symmetry. x1y1+⋯+xnyn=y1x1+⋯+ynxnx_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n = y_1x_1 + \dots + y_nx_nx1​y1​+⋯+xn​yn​=y1​x1​+⋯+yn​xn​, because the product of real numbers is commutative.
  3. Positive definite. ⟨x,x⟩=x12+⋯+xn2\langle x, x\rangle = x_1^2 + \dots + x_n^2⟨x,x⟩=x12​+⋯+xn2​ is a sum of squares. If x≠0x \neq 0x=0, at least one coordinate xix_ixi​ is not zero, and then xi2>0x_i^2 > 0xi2​>0 makes the whole sum positive. □\square□

Try it yourself with the tool: drag uuu and vvv and look at the number u⋅vu \cdot vu⋅v. Look for a position in which it is zero (the vectors are perpendicular) and one in which it is negative (obtuse angle). The tool also already shows the angle and the projection, which you will see in lessons L20 and L21.

Beyond the handouts · The scalar product of physics

In physics the scalar product of two vectors of the plane or of space is defined with lengths and angles: ⟨v,w⟩=∥v∥ ∥w∥cos⁡ϑ\langle v, w\rangle = \|v\|\,\|w\|\cos\vartheta⟨v,w⟩=∥v∥∥w∥cosϑ. The course goes the opposite way: first the scalar product, then (lesson L20) length ∥v∥=⟨v,v⟩\|v\| = \sqrt{\langle v, v\rangle}∥v∥=⟨v,v⟩​ and angle. The advantage is that the same construction works for very different spaces, like that of polynomials.

§6

Symmetric matrices and scalar products on Rn\R^nRn

pp. 97–98

In lesson L14 you saw that a square matrix AAA determines an endomorphism LA(x)=AxL_A(x) = AxLA​(x)=Ax of Rn\R^nRn. In the same way, a symmetric matrix determines a scalar product on Rn\R^nRn. Two reminders from lesson L08:

  • a matrix SSS is symmetric if it equals its transpose, tS=S{}^tS = StS=S, that is Sij=SjiS_{ij} = S_{ji}Sij​=Sji​ for every i,ji, ji,j: the part above the diagonal is the mirror image of the part below;
  • the transpose of a product is the product of the transposes in reverse order: t(AB)=tB tA{}^t(AB) = {}^tB\,{}^tAt(AB)=tBtA.

Proposition 19.7

A symmetric matrix SSS defines a scalar product gSg_SgS​ on Rn\R^nRn by setting

gS(x,y)=tx S y.g_S(x, y) = {}^tx\,S\,y.gS​(x,y)=txSy.

The proof, with all the steps:

  1. It is a number. tx{}^txtx is 1×n1 \times n1×n, SSS is n×nn \times nn×n, yyy is n×1n \times 1n×1: the product can be done and gives a 1×11 \times 11×1 matrix, a number.
  2. Bilinearity. It comes from the properties of the matrix product (distributivity, and scalars come out). For example t(x+x′) S y=tx S y+tx′ S y{}^t(x + x')\,S\,y = {}^tx\,S\,y + {}^tx'\,S\,yt(x+x′)Sy=txSy+tx′Sy.
  3. Symmetry. This is the chain of the handouts:
    gS(x,y)=tx S y=t(tx S y)=ty tS x=ty S x=gS(y,x).\begin{aligned} g_S(x, y) = {}^tx\,S\,y &= {}^t\big({}^tx\,S\,y\big) \\ &= {}^ty\,{}^tS\,x = {}^ty\,S\,x = g_S(y, x). \end{aligned}gS​(x,y)=txSy​=t(txSy)=tytSx=tySx=gS​(y,x).​
    • the second equals sign holds because tx S y{}^tx\,S\,ytxSy is a 1×11 \times 11×1 matrix, and a 1×11 \times 11×1 matrix is equal to its transpose;
    • the third uses t(ABC)=tC tB tA{}^t(ABC) = {}^tC\,{}^tB\,{}^tAt(ABC)=tCtBtA (the rule t(AB)=tB tA{}^t(AB) = {}^tB\,{}^tAt(AB)=tBtA applied twice) and t(tx)=x{}^t({}^tx) = xt(tx)=x;
    • the fourth uses precisely the hypothesis tS=S{}^tS = StS=S. Without symmetry of SSS the chain stops there. □\square□

To do the computations it is convenient to expand the matrix product.

Proposition 19.8

We have

gS(x,y)=tx S y=∑i,j=1nxiSijyj.g_S(x, y) = {}^tx\,S\,y = \sum_{i,j=1}^n x_iS_{ij}y_j.gS​(x,y)=txSy=i,j=1∑n​xi​Sij​yj​.

Indeed coordinate iii of the vector SySySy is (Sy)i=∑jSijyj(Sy)_i = \sum_{j} S_{ij}y_j(Sy)i​=∑j​Sij​yj​ (row iii of SSS times the column yyy), and then tx (Sy)=∑ixi(Sy)i=∑i,jxiSijyj{}^tx\,(Sy) = \sum_i x_i(Sy)_i = \sum_{i,j} x_iS_{ij}y_jtx(Sy)=∑i​xi​(Sy)i​=∑i,j​xi​Sij​yj​.

The double sum ∑i,j=1n\sum_{i,j=1}^n∑i,j=1n​ has one term for each pair (i,j)(i, j)(i,j): n2n^2n2 terms. For n=2n = 2n=2 and S=(abbc)S = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{pmatrix}S=(ab​bc​):

gS(x,y)=a x1y1+b x1y2+b x2y1+c x2y2.g_S(x, y) = a\,x_1y_1 + b\,x_1y_2 + b\,x_2y_1 + c\,x_2y_2.gS​(x,y)=ax1​y1​+bx1​y2​+bx2​y1​+cx2​y2​.

Corollary 19.9

For the vectors of the canonical basis we have

gS(ei,ej)=Sij.g_S(e_i, e_j) = S_{ij}.gS​(ei​,ej​)=Sij​.

The reason: eie_iei​ has a 1 in position iii and zeros elsewhere. In the sum of Proposition 19.8 with x=eix = e_ix=ei​ and y=ejy = e_jy=ej​ only one term survives, the one with xi=1x_i = 1xi​=1 and yj=1y_j = 1yj​=1, which equals SijS_{ij}Sij​. Example 19.10 · The identity matrix

For S=InS = I_nS=In​ you get the Euclidean scalar product:

gIn(x,y)=tx y=x1y1+⋯+xnyn.g_{I_n}(x, y) = {}^tx\,y = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n.gIn​​(x,y)=txy=x1​y1​+⋯+xn​yn​.

Example 19.11 · A non-diagonal matrix

The matrix

S=(2111)S = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}S=(21​11​)

defines on R2\R^2R2 the scalar product

gS(x,y)=2x1y1+x1y2+x2y1+x2y2.g_S(x, y) = 2x_1y_1 + x_1y_2 + x_2y_1 + x_2y_2.gS​(x,y)=2x1​y1​+x1​y2​+x2​y1​+x2​y2​.

Two computations: gS(e1,e2)=S12=1g_S(e_1, e_2) = S_{12} = 1gS​(e1​,e2​)=S12​=1 (so e1e_1e1​ and e2e_2e2​ do not give zero, unlike in the Euclidean product); with x=y=(1,−1)x = y = (1, -1)x=y=(1,−1): gS=2⋅1+1⋅(−1)+(−1)⋅1+(−1)⋅(−1)=2−1−1+1=1g_S = 2 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot (-1) + (-1) \cdot 1 + (-1) \cdot (-1) = 2 - 1 - 1 + 1 = 1gS​=2⋅1+1⋅(−1)+(−1)⋅1+(−1)⋅(−1)=2−1−1+1=1.

A sum of two squares is ≥0\ge 0≥0 and it is 0 only if x1=0x_1 = 0x1​=0 and x1+x2=0x_1 + x_2 = 0x1​+x2​=0, that is if x=0x = 0x=0. So yes.

From the formula to the matrix and back

Method · Between SSS and the formula of gSg_SgS​

From the matrix to the formula. For each entry SijS_{ij}Sij​ write the term Sij xiyjS_{ij}\,x_iy_jSij​xi​yj​ and add everything up. Zero entries give no terms.

From the formula to the matrix.

  1. Check that every term is of the form (number) ⋅ xiyj\cdot\, x_iy_j⋅xi​yj​, with one xxx and one yyy. Terms like x1x_1x1​, 111, x1x2x_1x_2x1​x2​, x12y1x_1^2y_1x12​y1​ mean that the formula is not bilinear.
  2. Put the coefficient of xiyjx_iy_jxi​yj​ in position (i,j)(i, j)(i,j).
  3. Check that the matrix is symmetric: the coefficient of xiyjx_iy_jxi​yj​ must be equal to that of xjyix_jy_ixj​yi​. If it is not, the formula is not a scalar product.

Example · There and back

  • g(x,y)=3x1y1−2x1y2−2x2y1+5x2y2g(x, y) = 3x_1y_1 - 2x_1y_2 - 2x_2y_1 + 5x_2y_2g(x,y)=3x1​y1​−2x1​y2​−2x2​y1​+5x2​y2​ has matrix S=(3−2−25)S = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}S=(3−2​−25​): the coefficient of x1y2x_1y_2x1​y2​ goes in position (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2), that of x2y1x_2y_1x2​y1​ in position (2,1)(2, 1)(2,1), and they are equal.
  • The matrix S=(12020−10−13)S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}S=​120​20−1​0−13​​ gives on R3\R^3R3
    gS(x,y)=x1y1+2x1y2+2x2y1−x2y3−x3y2+3x3y3.\begin{aligned} g_S(x, y) = {} & x_1y_1 + 2x_1y_2 + 2x_2y_1 \\ & - x_2y_3 - x_3y_2 + 3x_3y_3. \end{aligned}gS​(x,y)=​x1​y1​+2x1​y2​+2x2​y1​−x2​y3​−x3​y2​+3x3​y3​.​
  • g(x,y)=x1y2+2x2y1g(x, y) = x_1y_2 + 2x_2y_1g(x,y)=x1​y2​+2x2​y1​ is not a scalar product: it would put 1 in position (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) and 2 in position (2,1)(2, 1)(2,1), and the matrix would not be symmetric.

Pitfall · Do not divide by two

In the scalar product gS(x,y)g_S(x, y)gS​(x,y) the terms x1y2x_1y_2x1​y2​ and x2y1x_2y_1x2​y1​ are different and each one has its own position: the coefficient goes into the matrix as it is. Dividing by two is needed for the quadratic forms of lesson L20, where x1x2x_1x_2x1​x2​ and x2x1x_2x_1x2​x1​ are the same monomial.

When gSg_SgS​ is degenerate or positive definite (beyond the handouts)

Beyond the handouts · Three convenient criteria

1. Degenerate if and only if det⁡S=0\det S = 0detS=0 (Martelli, Proposition 7.1.23). If Sv=0Sv = 0Sv=0 with v≠0v \neq 0v=0, then for every www

gS(v,w)=tv S w=t(Sv) w=0,g_S(v, w) = {}^tv\,S\,w = {}^t(Sv)\,w = 0,gS​(v,w)=tvSw=t(Sv)w=0,

because t(Sv)=tv tS=tv S{}^t(Sv) = {}^tv\,{}^tS = {}^tv\,St(Sv)=tvtS=tvS. So gSg_SgS​ is degenerate. Conversely, if gS(v,w)=0g_S(v, w) = 0gS​(v,w)=0 for every www, take w=Svw = Svw=Sv: you get t(Sv)(Sv)=0{}^t(Sv)(Sv) = 0t(Sv)(Sv)=0, that is ⟨Sv,Sv⟩=0\langle Sv, Sv\rangle = 0⟨Sv,Sv⟩=0 in the Euclidean product, so Sv=0Sv = 0Sv=0. In short: gSg_SgS​ is degenerate   ⟺  \iff⟺ there is v≠0v \neq 0v=0 with Sv=0Sv = 0Sv=0   ⟺  \iff⟺ det⁡S=0\det S = 0detS=0 (lesson L10). The vectors that give zero with everything are those of the kernel of SSS.

2. Diagonal matrices (Martelli, §7.1.6). If SSS is diagonal with d1,…,dnd_1, \dots, d_nd1​,…,dn​ on the diagonal, then gS(x,x)=d1x12+⋯+dnxn2g_S(x, x) = d_1x_1^2 + \dots + d_nx_n^2gS​(x,x)=d1​x12​+⋯+dn​xn2​: gSg_SgS​ is positive definite   ⟺  \iff⟺ all the di>0d_i > 0di​>0, and it is non-degenerate   ⟺  \iff⟺ all the di≠0d_i \neq 0di​=0. §7

The matrix associated with a scalar product

pp. 98–99

For linear maps (lesson L15), once a basis is fixed, every map becomes a matrix. With scalar products the same happens.

Definition 19.12 · Associated matrix

Let VVV be a real vector space, let g:V×V→Rg : V \times V \to \Rg:V×V→R be a scalar product and let B={v1,…,vn}\mathcal B = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}B={v1​,…,vn​} be a basis of VVV. The matrix associated with ggg in the basis B\mathcal BB is the symmetric matrix

S=[g]B,Sij=g(vi,vj).S = [g]_{\mathcal B}, \qquad S_{ij} = g(v_i, v_j).S=[g]B​,Sij​=g(vi​,vj​).

Piece by piece:

  • the matrix is n×nn \times nn×n, with n=dim⁡Vn = \dim Vn=dimV: one row and one column for each vector of the basis;
  • in position (i,j)(i, j)(i,j) there is the scalar product between the iii-th and the jjj-th vector of the basis;
  • on the diagonal there are the products g(vi,vi)g(v_i, v_i)g(vi​,vi​) of each vector with itself;
  • it is symmetric because g(vi,vj)=g(vj,vi)g(v_i, v_j) = g(v_j, v_i)g(vi​,vj​)=g(vj​,vi​) (axiom 3);
  • it depends on the basis: same product, different basis, different matrix. How it changes you will see in lesson L20.

Example 19.13 · The canonical basis

If S∈M(n,R)S \in M(n, \R)S∈M(n,R) is symmetric, the matrix associated with gSg_SgS​ with respect to the canonical basis C\mathcal CC is SSS itself:

[gS]C=S.[g_S]_{\mathcal C} = S.[gS​]C​=S.

It is Corollary 19.9: the entry (i,j)(i, j)(i,j) of [gS]C[g_S]_{\mathcal C}[gS​]C​ is gS(ei,ej)=Sijg_S(e_i, e_j) = S_{ij}gS​(ei​,ej​)=Sij​.

Example 19.14 · The Euclidean product in another basis

Consider the Euclidean scalar product on R2\R^2R2 and the basis

B={v1=(10),v2=(11)}.\mathcal B = \left\{ v_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, v_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}.B={v1​=(10​),v2​=(11​)}.

The associated matrix is

[g]B=(g(v1,v1)g(v1,v2)g(v2,v1)g(v2,v2))=(1112).[g]_{\mathcal B} = \begin{pmatrix} g(v_1, v_1) & g(v_1, v_2) \\ g(v_2, v_1) & g(v_2, v_2) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.[g]B​=(g(v1​,v1​)g(v2​,v1​)​g(v1​,v2​)g(v2​,v2​)​)=(11​12​).

The computations: g(v1,v1)=1+0=1g(v_1, v_1) = 1 + 0 = 1g(v1​,v1​)=1+0=1, g(v1,v2)=1⋅1+0⋅1=1g(v_1, v_2) = 1 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 1 = 1g(v1​,v2​)=1⋅1+0⋅1=1, g(v2,v2)=1+1=2g(v_2, v_2) = 1 + 1 = 2g(v2​,v2​)=1+1=2. In the canonical basis the same product has matrix I2I_2I2​.

Why is the associated matrix useful? Because it contains all the information about the product: knowing the products between the vectors of the basis, you can compute the product of any two vectors.

Proposition 19.15

If

v=λ1v1+⋯+λnvn,w=μ1v1+⋯+μnvn,v = \lambda_1v_1 + \dots + \lambda_nv_n, \qquad w = \mu_1v_1 + \dots + \mu_nv_n,v=λ1​v1​+⋯+λn​vn​,w=μ1​v1​+⋯+μn​vn​,

then

g(v,w)=∑i,j=1nλiμj g(vi,vj).g(v, w) = \sum_{i,j=1}^n \lambda_i\mu_j\,g(v_i, v_j).g(v,w)=i,j=1∑n​λi​μj​g(vi​,vj​).

The formula follows from bilinearity: you "expand" it like a product of two sums. With n=2n = 2n=2, one step at a time. First linearity in the first slot (axioms 1 and 2), keeping w=μ1v1+μ2v2w = \mu_1v_1 + \mu_2v_2w=μ1​v1​+μ2​v2​ fixed:

g(λ1v1+λ2v2, w)=λ1 g(v1,w)+λ2 g(v2,w).g(\lambda_1v_1 + \lambda_2v_2,\ w) = \lambda_1\,g(v_1, w) + \lambda_2\,g(v_2, w).g(λ1​v1​+λ2​v2​, w)=λ1​g(v1​,w)+λ2​g(v2​,w).

Then linearity in the second slot (axioms 4 and 5) inside each term:

g(v1,w)=μ1 g(v1,v1)+μ2 g(v1,v2),g(v2,w)=μ1 g(v2,v1)+μ2 g(v2,v2).\begin{aligned} g(v_1, w) &= \mu_1\,g(v_1, v_1) + \mu_2\,g(v_1, v_2), \\ g(v_2, w) &= \mu_1\,g(v_2, v_1) + \mu_2\,g(v_2, v_2). \end{aligned}g(v1​,w)g(v2​,w)​=μ1​g(v1​,v1​)+μ2​g(v1​,v2​),=μ1​g(v2​,v1​)+μ2​g(v2​,v2​).​

Putting it together:

g(v,w)=λ1μ1 g(v1,v1)+λ1μ2 g(v1,v2)+λ2μ1 g(v2,v1)+λ2μ2 g(v2,v2).\begin{aligned} g(v, w) = {} & \lambda_1\mu_1\,g(v_1, v_1) + \lambda_1\mu_2\,g(v_1, v_2) \\ & + \lambda_2\mu_1\,g(v_2, v_1) + \lambda_2\mu_2\,g(v_2, v_2). \end{aligned}g(v,w)=​λ1​μ1​g(v1​,v1​)+λ1​μ2​g(v1​,v2​)+λ2​μ1​g(v2​,v1​)+λ2​μ2​g(v2​,v2​).​

There are four terms, one for each pair (i,j)(i, j)(i,j).

Corollary 19.16

For every v,w∈Vv, w \in Vv,w∈V we have

g(v,w)=t[v]B [g]B [w]B.g(v, w) = {}^t[v]_{\mathcal B}\,[g]_{\mathcal B}\,[w]_{\mathcal B}.g(v,w)=t[v]B​[g]B​[w]B​.

Here [v]B=(λ1,…,λn)[v]_{\mathcal B} = (\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)[v]B​=(λ1​,…,λn​) is the column vector of the coordinates of vvv in the basis B\mathcal BB (lesson L15). The row-matrix-column product, expanded with Proposition 19.8, gives exactly the sum of Proposition 19.15. In words: in coordinates, every scalar product becomes a gSg_SgS​, with SSS the associated matrix.

Computing with coordinates

Euclidean product on R2\R^2R2, basis B={(1,0),(1,1)}\mathcal B = \{(1, 0), (1, 1)\}B={(1,0),(1,1)} and [g]B=(1112)[g]_{\mathcal B} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}[g]B​=(11​12​) (Example 19.14). Take v=(3,2)v = (3, 2)v=(3,2) and w=(1,−1)w = (1, -1)w=(1,−1).

First [g]B[w]B=(1⋅2+1⋅(−1)1⋅2+2⋅(−1))=(10)[g]_{\mathcal B}[w]_{\mathcal B} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot (-1) \\ 1 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot (-1) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}[g]B​[w]B​=(1⋅2+1⋅(−1)1⋅2+2⋅(−1)​)=(10​), then t(1,2)(10)=1{}^t(1, 2)\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = 1t(1,2)(10​)=1.
  4. Direct check. ⟨(3,2),(1,−1)⟩=3−2=1\langle (3, 2), (1, -1)\rangle = 3 - 2 = 1⟨(3,2),(1,−1)⟩=3−2=1. ✓

Method · Computing [g]B[g]_{\mathcal B}[g]B​

  1. Write the vectors of the basis in the given order: the order decides rows and columns.
  2. If ggg is defined on polynomials by evaluating at some points, first compute the table of the values of each viv_ivi​ at those points.
  3. Compute g(vi,vj)g(v_i, v_j)g(vi​,vj​) for i≤ji \le ji≤j: that is n(n+1)2\frac{n(n+1)}22n(n+1)​ computations (3 for n=2n = 2n=2, 6 for n=3n = 3n=3).
  4. Fill in the matrix and copy the entries above the diagonal into those below.
  5. Check: if g=gSg = g_Sg=gS​ on Rn\R^nRn, the entry (i,j)(i, j)(i,j) is tvi S vj{}^tv_i\,S\,v_jtvi​Svj​; compute the columns SvjSv_jSvj​ only once and reuse them.

Beyond the handouts · Where to find it in the book

Martelli, chapter 7 "Prodotti scalari": §7.1.1–7.1.3 (definition, degenerate and positive definite, Euclidean product, pp. 199–201), §7.1.4 (symmetric matrices, pp. 201–203), §7.1.6 (diagonal matrices, pp. 204–205), §7.1.10 (the products on polynomials of Example 19.4, p. 209), §7.2.1 (associated matrix, pp. 210–212). In the book you also find the words isotropic vector (§7.1.8) and radical (§7.1.9), which the handouts do not use.

§8

Towards the exam

exam

The written test of Linear Algebra and Geometry has 10 multiple-choice questions (5 answers, one right) and 2 problems worth 11 points, marked only with at least 6 points in the quiz; it lasts 2 hours, with no calculator, and only 4 handwritten pages of notes. 2026/27 exam sessions: 22/01 and 05/02/2027, at 14:00. The details are in lesson L01.

What of this lesson appears in the 2023–2026 exam sessions

  1. The associated matrix in a basis (quiz). It is the most frequent question: in the exam sessions of 24/01/2024 (question 7), 10/07/2024 (question 9) and 15/01/2026 (question 9) the product is given by an unusual formula on R1[x]\R_1[x]R1​[x] or on R2\R^2R2, and you must find [g]B[g]_{\mathcal B}[g]B​ among five matrices. In the exam sessions of 10/06/2024 (question 4) and 03/06/2026 (question 4) you are given gSg_SgS​ with SSS of order 3 and a new basis: you work entry by entry or with the formula tMSM{}^tMSMtMSM of lesson L20.
  2. The first part of the problems. In problems 12 of 16/01/2025, 07/02/2025 and 05/02/2026 part (1) asks for the associated matrix (in the canonical basis of R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x] or in a basis of R3\R^3R3); the following parts use norms, angles, Gram–Schmidt and projections (lessons L20 and L21).
  3. Theory. Telling apart degenerate, non-degenerate and positive definite; knowing that gSg_SgS​ is a scalar product only if SSS is symmetric.

Three real exam questions, solved

Example · Exam of 15/01/2026, question 9

Given x=t(x1,x2)x = {}^t(x_1, x_2)x=t(x1​,x2​) and y=t(y1,y2)y = {}^t(y_1, y_2)y=t(y1​,y2​), let g(x,y)=x1y2+x2y1−x2y2g(x, y) = x_1y_2 + x_2y_1 - x_2y_2g(x,y)=x1​y2​+x2​y1​−x2​y2​. Given the basis B={t(1,1),t(0,1)}\mathcal B = \{{}^t(1, 1), {}^t(0, 1)\}B={t(1,1),t(0,1)}, what is [g]B[g]_{\mathcal B}[g]B​?

Solution. v1=(1,1)v_1 = (1, 1)v1​=(1,1), v2=(0,1)v_2 = (0, 1)v2​=(0,1).

  • g(v1,v1)=1⋅1+1⋅1−1⋅1=1g(v_1, v_1) = 1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot 1 = 1g(v1​,v1​)=1⋅1+1⋅1−1⋅1=1;
  • g(v1,v2)g(v_1, v_2)g(v1​,v2​) with x=(1,1)x = (1, 1)x=(1,1), y=(0,1)y = (0, 1)y=(0,1): 1⋅1+1⋅0−1⋅1=01 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 1 = 01⋅1+1⋅0−1⋅1=0;
  • g(v2,v2)g(v_2, v_2)g(v2​,v2​) with x=y=(0,1)x = y = (0, 1)x=y=(0,1): 0+0−1=−10 + 0 - 1 = -10+0−1=−1.

So [g]B=(100−1)[g]_{\mathcal B} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}[g]B​=(10​0−1​) (answer (a)). Note: the product is non-degenerate but not positive definite, because g(v2,v2)=−1g(v_2, v_2) = -1g(v2​,v2​)=−1.

Example · Exam of 24/01/2024, question 7

On R1[x]\R_1[x]R1​[x] you are given the scalar product g(p,q)=q(1)p(1)−q(0)p(0)g(p, q) = q(1)p(1) - q(0)p(0)g(p,q)=q(1)p(1)−q(0)p(0) and the basis B={x+1,2}\mathcal B = \{x + 1, 2\}B={x+1,2}. What is [g]B[g]_{\mathcal B}[g]B​?

Solution. Table of values: x+1x + 1x+1 equals 222 at 1 and 111 at 0; the constant polynomial 222 equals 222 at both points.

  • g(x+1,x+1)=2⋅2−1⋅1=3g(x + 1, x + 1) = 2 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 1 = 3g(x+1,x+1)=2⋅2−1⋅1=3;
  • g(x+1,2)=2⋅2−1⋅2=2g(x + 1, 2) = 2 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 2 = 2g(x+1,2)=2⋅2−1⋅2=2;
  • g(2,2)=2⋅2−2⋅2=0g(2, 2) = 2 \cdot 2 - 2 \cdot 2 = 0g(2,2)=2⋅2−2⋅2=0.

So [g]B=(3220)[g]_{\mathcal B} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}[g]B​=(32​20​) (answer (a)). Answer (e), (3110)\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}(31​10​), is the one you get by mistakenly using the polynomial 111 instead of 222: the second vector of the basis equals 2, not 1.

Example · Exam of 07/02/2025, problem 12, part (1)

On R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x] we define g(p,q)=p(1)q(1)+p(−1)q(−1)+p(1)q(0)+p(0)q(1)+2p(0)q(0)g(p, q) = p(1)q(1) + p(-1)q(-1) + p(1)q(0) + p(0)q(1) + 2p(0)q(0)g(p,q)=p(1)q(1)+p(−1)q(−1)+p(1)q(0)+p(0)q(1)+2p(0)q(0). Find the matrix associated with ggg in the canonical basis {1,x,x2}\{1, x, x^2\}{1,x,x2}.

Solution. Values at 1,−1,01, -1, 01,−1,0: 1→(1,1,1)1 \to (1, 1, 1)1→(1,1,1), x→(1,−1,0)x \to (1, -1, 0)x→(1,−1,0), x2→(1,1,0)x^2 \to (1, 1, 0)x2→(1,1,0). Then, term by term in the order of the formula:

  • g(1,1)=1+1+1+1+2=6g(1, 1) = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 6g(1,1)=1+1+1+1+2=6;
  • g(1,x)=1⋅1+1⋅(−1)+1⋅0+1⋅1+2⋅1⋅0=1g(1, x) = 1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot (-1) + 1 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 0 = 1g(1,x)=1⋅1+1⋅(−1)+1⋅0+1⋅1+2⋅1⋅0=1;
  • g(1,x2)=1+1+0+1+0=3g(1, x^2) = 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 3g(1,x2)=1+1+0+1+0=3;
  • g(x,x)=1+1+0+0+0=2g(x, x) = 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 2g(x,x)=1+1+0+0+0=2;
  • g(x,x2)=1⋅1+(−1)⋅1+1⋅0+0⋅1+0=0g(x, x^2) = 1 \cdot 1 + (-1) \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 1 + 0 = 0g(x,x2)=1⋅1+(−1)⋅1+1⋅0+0⋅1+0=0;
  • g(x2,x2)=1+1+0+0+0=2g(x^2, x^2) = 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 2g(x2,x2)=1+1+0+0+0=2.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Mixing up the order of the vectors of the basis: [g]{v1,v2}[g]_{\{v_1, v_2\}}[g]{v1​,v2​}​ and [g]{v2,v1}[g]_{\{v_2, v_1\}}[g]{v2​,v1​}​ have the diagonal entries swapped.
  • In products on polynomials, getting a value wrong: write the table of values first, then do the products.
  • Forgetting that the associated matrix is always symmetric: in the quiz discard the non-symmetric matrices at once.
  • Dividing the mixed coefficients of g(x,y)g(x, y)g(x,y) by two: you divide only for quadratic forms (lesson L20).

1 · Scalar product or not? basic

For each formula on R2\R^2R2 say whether it is a scalar product; if it is not, indicate a rule that fails with a numerical example. (a) 2x1y1+3x2y22x_1y_1 + 3x_2y_22x1​y1​+3x2​y2​; (b) x1y2x_1y_2x1​y2​; (c) x1y1+x2y2+1x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 + 1x1​y1​+x2​y2​+1; (d) x1y1−4x1y2−4x2y1+x2y2x_1y_1 - 4x_1y_2 - 4x_2y_1 + x_2y_2x1​y1​−4x1​y2​−4x2​y1​+x2​y2​; (e) x12y12x_1^2y_1^2x12​y12​.

Solution

(a) Yes. It is gSg_SgS​ with S=(2003)S = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}S=(20​03​), which is symmetric (Proposition 19.7). The axioms are checked one by one in the example of the section on the definition.

(b) No, it is not symmetric: g(e1,e2)=1⋅1=1g(e_1, e_2) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1g(e1​,e2​)=1⋅1=1 but g(e2,e1)=0⋅0=0g(e_2, e_1) = 0 \cdot 0 = 0g(e2​,e1​)=0⋅0=0.

(c) No, it is not bilinear: g(0,0)=1g(0, 0) = 1g(0,0)=1, while ⟨v,0⟩=0\langle v, 0\rangle = 0⟨v,0⟩=0 must hold.

(d) Yes. Every term has one xxx and one yyy, and the coefficients of x1y2x_1y_2x1​y2​ and x2y1x_2y_1x2​y1​ are equal: it is gSg_SgS​ with S=(1−4−41)S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -4 \\ -4 & 1 \end{pmatrix}S=(1−4​−41​), which is symmetric. (It is not positive definite: g((1,1),(1,1))=1−4−4+1=−6g((1, 1), (1, 1)) = 1 - 4 - 4 + 1 = -6g((1,1),(1,1))=1−4−4+1=−6.)

(e) No, it is not linear in the first slot: g(2e1,e1)=4⋅1=4g(2e_1, e_1) = 4 \cdot 1 = 4g(2e1​,e1​)=4⋅1=4, while 2 g(e1,e1)=22\,g(e_1, e_1) = 22g(e1​,e1​)=2.

2 · Computations with the Euclidean product basic

(a) Compute ⟨(2,−1,3),(1,4,1)⟩\langle (2, -1, 3), (1, 4, 1)\rangle⟨(2,−1,3),(1,4,1)⟩. (b) Compute ⟨(1,1,1,1),(1,−1,1,−1)⟩\langle (1, 1, 1, 1), (1, -1, 1, -1)\rangle⟨(1,1,1,1),(1,−1,1,−1)⟩. (c) Find k∈Rk \in \Rk∈R such that ⟨(1,k,2),(3,1,−k)⟩=0\langle (1, k, 2), (3, 1, -k)\rangle = 0⟨(1,k,2),(3,1,−k)⟩=0.

Solution

(a) 2⋅1+(−1)⋅4+3⋅1=2−4+3=12 \cdot 1 + (-1) \cdot 4 + 3 \cdot 1 = 2 - 4 + 3 = 12⋅1+(−1)⋅4+3⋅1=2−4+3=1.

(b) 1−1+1−1=01 - 1 + 1 - 1 = 01−1+1−1=0: the two vectors of R4\R^4R4 are perpendicular.

(c) ⟨(1,k,2),(3,1,−k)⟩=1⋅3+k⋅1+2⋅(−k)=3+k−2k=3−k\langle (1, k, 2), (3, 1, -k)\rangle = 1 \cdot 3 + k \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot (-k) = 3 + k - 2k = 3 - k⟨(1,k,2),(3,1,−k)⟩=1⋅3+k⋅1+2⋅(−k)=3+k−2k=3−k. It is zero for k=3k = 3k=3. Check: ⟨(1,3,2),(3,1,−3)⟩=3+3−6=0\langle (1, 3, 2), (3, 1, -3)\rangle = 3 + 3 - 6 = 0⟨(1,3,2),(3,1,−3)⟩=3+3−6=0. ✓

3 · From the matrix to the formula and back basic

(a) Write gS(x,y)g_S(x, y)gS​(x,y) for S=(1−20−23404−1)S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & -1 \end{pmatrix}S=​1−20​−234​04−1​​. (b) Find the matrix of g(x,y)=x1y1+3x1y2+3x2y1−x2y2+2x1y3+2x3y1g(x, y) = x_1y_1 + 3x_1y_2 + 3x_2y_1 - x_2y_2 + 2x_1y_3 + 2x_3y_1g(x,y)=x1​y1​+3x1​y2​+3x2​y1​−x2​y2​+2x1​y3​+2x3​y1​ on R3\R^3R3. (c) Compute gS(e2,e3)g_S(e_2, e_3)gS​(e2​,e3​) for the matrix of part (a).

Solution

(a) One term SijxiyjS_{ij}x_iy_jSij​xi​yj​ for each non-zero entry:

gS(x,y)=x1y1−2x1y2−2x2y1+3x2y2+4x2y3+4x3y2−x3y3.\begin{aligned} g_S(x, y) = {} & x_1y_1 - 2x_1y_2 - 2x_2y_1 + 3x_2y_2 \\ & + 4x_2y_3 + 4x_3y_2 - x_3y_3. \end{aligned}gS​(x,y)=​x1​y1​−2x1​y2​−2x2​y1​+3x2​y2​+4x2​y3​+4x3​y2​−x3​y3​.​

(b) The coefficient of xiyjx_iy_jxi​yj​ goes in position (i,j)(i, j)(i,j); the terms with x2y3x_2y_3x2​y3​, x3y2x_3y_2x3​y2​, x3y3x_3y_3x3​y3​ are missing, so those entries are 0:

S=(1323−10200).S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.S=​132​3−10​200​​.

It is symmetric, so the formula really is a scalar product.

(c) By Corollary 19.9, gS(e2,e3)=S23=4g_S(e_2, e_3) = S_{23} = 4gS​(e2​,e3​)=S23​=4.

4 · Degenerate, positive definite or neither? intermediate

For each matrix say whether gSg_SgS​ on R2\R^2R2 is degenerate, positive definite, or non-degenerate but not positive definite:

S1=(1224),S2=(1225),S3=(1223).S_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad S_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad S_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}.S1​=(12​24​),S2​=(12​25​),S3​=(12​23​).
Solution

S1S_1S1​: degenerate. I look for v≠0v \neq 0v=0 with S1v=0S_1v = 0S1​v=0: x1+2x2=0x_1 + 2x_2 = 0x1​+2x2​=0 (the second row is twice the first), for example v=(2,−1)v = (2, -1)v=(2,−1): S1v=(2−2,4−4)=(0,0)S_1v = (2 - 2, 4 - 4) = (0, 0)S1​v=(2−2,4−4)=(0,0). Then for every www: gS1(v,w)=t(S1v) w=0g_{S_1}(v, w) = {}^t(S_1v)\,w = 0gS1​​(v,w)=t(S1​v)w=0.

S2S_2S2​: positive definite. I complete the square:

gS2(x,x)=x12+4x1x2+5x22=(x12+4x1x2+4x22)+x22=(x1+2x2)2+x22.\begin{aligned} g_{S_2}(x, x) &= x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 + 5x_2^2 \\ &= (x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 + 4x_2^2) + x_2^2 = (x_1 + 2x_2)^2 + x_2^2. \end{aligned}gS2​​(x,x)​=x12​+4x1​x2​+5x22​=(x12​+4x1​x2​+4x22​)+x22​=(x1​+2x2​)2+x22​.​

It is ≥0\ge 0≥0 and it is 0 only if x2=0x_2 = 0x2​=0 and x1+2x2=0x_1 + 2x_2 = 0x1​+2x2​=0, that is x=0x = 0x=0. (With the 2×22 \times 22×2 criterion: a=1>0a = 1 > 0a=1>0, det⁡S2=1>0\det S_2 = 1 > 0detS2​=1>0.)

S3S_3S3​: non-degenerate, not positive definite. det⁡S3=3−4=−1≠0\det S_3 = 3 - 4 = -1 \neq 0detS3​=3−4=−1=0, so it is not degenerate (determinant criterion). But with x=(2,−1)x = (2, -1)x=(2,−1):

gS3(x,x)=x12+4x1x2+3x22=4−8+3=−1<0.g_{S_3}(x, x) = x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 + 3x_2^2 = 4 - 8 + 3 = -1 < 0.gS3​​(x,x)=x12​+4x1​x2​+3x22​=4−8+3=−1<0.

5 · A basis in which gSg_SgS​ looks Euclidean intermediate

Let S=(2111)S = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}S=(21​11​) (Example 19.11) and let B={v1=(1,−1), v2=(0,1)}\mathcal B = \{v_1 = (1, -1),\ v_2 = (0, 1)\}B={v1​=(1,−1), v2​=(0,1)}. Compute [gS]B[g_S]_{\mathcal B}[gS​]B​. What do you notice?

I use gS(x,y)=2x1y1+x1y2+x2y1+x2y2g_S(x, y) = 2x_1y_1 + x_1y_2 + x_2y_1 + x_2y_2gS​(x,y)=2x1​y1​+x1​y2​+x2​y1​+x2​y2​.

In this basis the product gSg_SgS​ has the same matrix as the Euclidean product in the canonical basis: in coordinates, gS(v,w)=λ1μ1+λ2μ2g_S(v, w) = \lambda_1\mu_1 + \lambda_2\mu_2gS​(v,w)=λ1​μ1​+λ2​μ2​. §11

Review questions

self-check

Answer out loud or in writing, then open the answer.

What is a scalar product on a real vector space VVV?

A map V×V→RV \times V \to \RV×V→R, (v,w)↦⟨v,w⟩(v, w) \mapsto \langle v, w\rangle(v,w)↦⟨v,w⟩, which is linear in the first slot (⟨v+v′,w⟩=⟨v,w⟩+⟨v′,w⟩\langle v + v', w\rangle = \langle v, w\rangle + \langle v', w\rangle⟨v+v′,w⟩=⟨v,w⟩+⟨v′,w⟩ and ⟨λv,w⟩=λ⟨v,w⟩\langle \lambda v, w\rangle = \lambda\langle v, w\rangle⟨λv,w⟩=λ⟨v,w⟩) and symmetric (⟨v,w⟩=⟨w,v⟩\langle v, w\rangle = \langle w, v\rangle⟨v,w⟩=⟨w,v⟩). Linearity in the second slot follows from this: the product is bilinear.

Why is the field R\RR, and not C\CC or Q\QQ, in the lessons on scalar products?

Because you need positive numbers (to say ⟨v,v⟩>0\langle v, v\rangle > 0⟨v,v⟩>0), which make no sense in C\CC, and the square roots of positive numbers (for the length ⟨v,v⟩\sqrt{\langle v, v\rangle}⟨v,v⟩​), which are missing in Q\QQ.

How do you derive ⟨v,λw⟩=λ⟨v,w⟩\langle v, \lambda w\rangle = \lambda\langle v, w\rangle⟨v,λw⟩=λ⟨v,w⟩ from the axioms?

You turn round with symmetry, use the axiom on the first slot and turn round again: ⟨v,λw⟩=⟨λw,v⟩=λ⟨w,v⟩=λ⟨v,w⟩\langle v, \lambda w\rangle = \langle \lambda w, v\rangle = \lambda\langle w, v\rangle = \lambda\langle v, w\rangle⟨v,λw⟩=⟨λw,v⟩=λ⟨w,v⟩=λ⟨v,w⟩.

Why is ⟨v,0⟩=0\langle v, 0\rangle = 0⟨v,0⟩=0 for every vvv?

Because ⟨v,0⟩=⟨v,0+0⟩=⟨v,0⟩+⟨v,0⟩\langle v, 0\rangle = \langle v, 0 + 0\rangle = \langle v, 0\rangle + \langle v, 0\rangle⟨v,0⟩=⟨v,0+0⟩=⟨v,0⟩+⟨v,0⟩; taking ⟨v,0⟩\langle v, 0\rangle⟨v,0⟩ away from both sides, what is left is 0=⟨v,0⟩0 = \langle v, 0\rangle0=⟨v,0⟩.

What is the difference between "degenerate" and "positive definite"? Give an example of each.

Degenerate: there is v≠0v \neq 0v=0 with ⟨v,w⟩=0\langle v, w\rangle = 0⟨v,w⟩=0 for every www (example: x1y1x_1y_1x1​y1​ on R2\R^2R2, with v=e2v = e_2v=e2​). Positive definite: ⟨v,v⟩>0\langle v, v\rangle > 0⟨v,v⟩>0 for every v≠0v \neq 0v=0 (example: the Euclidean product). The first condition is about the product with all vectors, the second about the product of each vector with itself.

Why is a positive definite product not degenerate? Does the converse hold?

If there were v≠0v \neq 0v=0 with ⟨v,w⟩=0\langle v, w\rangle = 0⟨v,w⟩=0 for every www, with w=vw = vw=v you would have ⟨v,v⟩=0\langle v, v\rangle = 0⟨v,v⟩=0, against positive definiteness. The converse is false: x1y1−x2y2x_1y_1 - x_2y_2x1​y1​−x2​y2​ is non-degenerate but ⟨e2,e2⟩=−1\langle e_2, e_2\rangle = -1⟨e2​,e2​⟩=−1.

What is the Euclidean scalar product and why is it positive definite?

It is ⟨x,y⟩=tx y=x1y1+⋯+xnyn\langle x, y\rangle = {}^tx\,y = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n⟨x,y⟩=txy=x1​y1​+⋯+xn​yn​ on Rn\R^nRn. It is positive definite because ⟨x,x⟩=x12+⋯+xn2\langle x, x\rangle = x_1^2 + \dots + x_n^2⟨x,x⟩=x12​+⋯+xn2​ is a sum of squares, positive as soon as one coordinate is not zero.

How do you get a scalar product from a matrix? Why must the matrix be symmetric?

With gS(x,y)=tx S y=∑i,jxiSijyjg_S(x, y) = {}^tx\,S\,y = \sum_{i,j} x_iS_{ij}y_jgS​(x,y)=txSy=∑i,j​xi​Sij​yj​. Bilinearity comes from the matrix product; the symmetry gS(x,y)=gS(y,x)g_S(x, y) = g_S(y, x)gS​(x,y)=gS​(y,x) requires tS=S{}^tS = StS=S, because tx S y=ty tS x{}^tx\,S\,y = {}^ty\,{}^tS\,xtxSy=tytSx.

What is gS(ei,ej)g_S(e_i, e_j)gS​(ei​,ej​)? And how do you read the matrix off the formula of gSg_SgS​?

gS(ei,ej)=Sijg_S(e_i, e_j) = S_{ij}gS​(ei​,ej​)=Sij​: tei{}^te_itei​ picks row iii, eje_jej​ column jjj. As a consequence SijS_{ij}Sij​ is the coefficient of xiyjx_iy_jxi​yj​ in the formula, without dividing by two.

What is the associated matrix [g]B[g]_{\mathcal B}[g]B​? Why is it symmetric?

Once the basis B={v1,…,vn}\mathcal B = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}B={v1​,…,vn​} is fixed, it is the n×nn \times nn×n matrix with entry (i,j)(i, j)(i,j) equal to g(vi,vj)g(v_i, v_j)g(vi​,vj​). It is symmetric because g(vi,vj)=g(vj,vi)g(v_i, v_j) = g(v_j, v_i)g(vi​,vj​)=g(vj​,vi​).

How do you compute g(v,w)g(v, w)g(v,w) knowing [g]B[g]_{\mathcal B}[g]B​?

With coordinates: g(v,w)=t[v]B [g]B [w]Bg(v, w) = {}^t[v]_{\mathcal B}\,[g]_{\mathcal B}\,[w]_{\mathcal B}g(v,w)=t[v]B​[g]B​[w]B​ (Corollary 19.16). It comes from bilinearity: if v=∑λiviv = \sum \lambda_iv_iv=∑λi​vi​ and w=∑μjvjw = \sum \mu_jv_jw=∑μj​vj​, then g(v,w)=∑i,jλiμj g(vi,vj)g(v, w) = \sum_{i,j} \lambda_i\mu_j\,g(v_i, v_j)g(v,w)=∑i,j​λi​μj​g(vi​,vj​).

Why is p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)+p(2)q(2)p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1) + p(2)q(2)p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)+p(2)q(2) positive definite on R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x], while p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1)p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1) is degenerate?

In the first, ⟨p,p⟩=0\langle p, p\rangle = 0⟨p,p⟩=0 forces ppp to have three distinct roots, impossible for a non-zero polynomial of degree ≤2\le 2≤2. In the second two roots are enough: p=x(1−x)p = x(1 - x)p=x(1−x) is non-zero, vanishes at 0 and at 1, and so gives zero with every qqq.

Glossary

terms
Scalar product
Bilinear and symmetric map V×V→RV \times V \to \RV×V→R; it is written ⟨v,w⟩\langle v, w\rangle⟨v,w⟩ or g(v,w)g(v, w)g(v,w).
Bilinear
Linear in the first slot when the second is fixed, and linear in the second when the first is fixed.
Symmetric
⟨v,w⟩=⟨w,v⟩\langle v, w\rangle = \langle w, v\rangle⟨v,w⟩=⟨w,v⟩ for every v,wv, wv,w.
Degenerate
There is v≠0v \neq 0v=0 with ⟨v,w⟩=0\langle v, w\rangle = 0⟨v,w⟩=0 for every w∈Vw \in Vw∈V. For gSg_SgS​: it happens if and only if det⁡S=0\det S = 0detS=0.
Non-degenerate
For every v≠0v \neq 0v=0 there is www with ⟨v,w⟩≠0\langle v, w\rangle \neq 0⟨v,w⟩=0.
Positive definite
⟨v,v⟩>0\langle v, v\rangle > 0⟨v,v⟩>0 for every v≠0v \neq 0v=0. It implies non-degenerate.
Euclidean scalar product
On Rn\R^nRn: ⟨x,y⟩=tx y=x1y1+⋯+xnyn\langle x, y\rangle = {}^tx\,y = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n⟨x,y⟩=txy=x1​y1​+⋯+xn​yn​. It is positive definite.
Transpose tx{}^txtx
The column vector xxx written as a row; tx y{}^tx\,ytxy is a row-by-column product that gives a number.
Symmetric matrix
Square matrix with tS=S{}^tS = StS=S, that is Sij=SjiS_{ij} = S_{ji}Sij​=Sji​.
gSg_SgS​
The scalar product gS(x,y)=tx S y=∑i,jxiSijyjg_S(x, y) = {}^tx\,S\,y = \sum_{i,j} x_iS_{ij}y_jgS​(x,y)=txSy=∑i,j​xi​Sij​yj​ defined by a symmetric matrix SSS.
Canonical basis
e1,…,ene_1, \dots, e_ne1​,…,en​, with eie_iei​ having 1 in position iii and 0 elsewhere; gS(ei,ej)=Sijg_S(e_i, e_j) = S_{ij}gS​(ei​,ej​)=Sij​.
Associated matrix [g]B[g]_{\mathcal B}[g]B​
Symmetric matrix with entry (i,j)(i, j)(i,j) equal to g(vi,vj)g(v_i, v_j)g(vi​,vj​), where B={v1,…,vn}\mathcal B = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}B={v1​,…,vn​}.
Coordinates [v]B[v]_{\mathcal B}[v]B​
The coefficients λ1,…,λn\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_nλ1​,…,λn​ with v=λ1v1+⋯+λnvnv = \lambda_1v_1 + \dots + \lambda_nv_nv=λ1​v1​+⋯+λn​vn​, written as a column.
Rk[x]\R_k[x]Rk​[x]
The space of polynomials with real coefficients of degree ≤k\le k≤k; it has dimension k+1k + 1k+1 and canonical basis {1,x,…,xk}\{1, x, \dots, x^k\}{1,x,…,xk}.
Isotropic vector
(Martelli's term.) Vector vvv with ⟨v,v⟩=0\langle v, v\rangle = 0⟨v,v⟩=0; if the product is positive definite the only one is v=0v = 0v=0.
Radical
(Martelli's term.) The set of vectors that give zero with everything; for gSg_SgS​ it is the kernel of SSS. It is {0}\{0\}{0} exactly when the product is non-degenerate.

Sources and notes

  • 2026 course handouts (Buzano, Radeschi), lesson 19 "Prodotti scalari I", pp. 96–99: sections 19.A (definitions), 19.B (symmetric matrices) and 19.C (associated matrix) are followed in order, with the same numbering (Definitions 19.1, 19.2, 19.5, 19.12; Propositions 19.3, 19.6, 19.7, 19.8, 19.15; Corollaries 19.9, 19.16; Examples 19.4, 19.10, 19.11, 19.13, 19.14). The handouts have no exercises for this lesson. Reminders from other lessons: Theorem 4.6 (roots of a polynomial), lessons L08 (transpose), L10 (determinant), L15 (coordinates).
  • B. Martelli, Geometria e algebra lineare, chapter 7: §7.1 (in particular the proof of Proposition 7.1.5, the criteria for diagonal matrices of §7.1.6, Proposition 7.1.23 on the radical and the words "isotropo" and "radicale") and §7.2.1 (associated matrix). The book is free: people.dm.unipi.it/martelli.

The three questions reported are solved in these notes.
  • The "Beyond the handouts" parts (the square of a sum, the non-degeneracy of the third product of Example 19.4, the product of physics, the criteria with the determinant, diagonal matrices and the 2×22 \times 22×2 criterion) and all the exercises are additions in these notes, to connect the lesson to the rest of the course and to the exam.
